After process_raw_file_for_config applies every inline "-- sqlfluff:" directive (through process_inline_config, which updates the string-valued `rules` and `exclude_rules` settings), it calls `_handle_comma_separated_values()`. That method rebuilds the list forms `rule_allowlist` and `rule_denylist` by splitting the current `rules` and `exclude_rules` strings. The functional wrappers are `FunctionalContext` and `Segments`. `FunctionalContext` (context.py) wraps a `RuleContext`. Its properties (`segment`, `parent_stack`, `siblings_pre`, `siblings_post`, `raw_stack`, `raw_segments`) each return a `Segments` object. `Segments` (segments.py:20) is a `tuple[BaseSegment, ...]` subclass. LT09 (the layout rule that enforces select targets on a new line) imports `FunctionalContext`, `Segments` and `sp`. It therefore works through this layer instead of walking `BaseSegment` trees by hand with indexing and loops. The wrappers act as an adapter or facade between the rules and the parse tree. Rule code is written as declarative queries, such as `children(sp.is_type(...))`. Knowledge of how the tree is structured stays inside the wrapper layer. I did not open LT09's body, so this is based on its imports and on the wrapper code.

In the Exasol dialect, RejectClauseSegment.match_grammar is a Sequence("REJECT", "LIMIT", OneOf(Ref("NumericLiteralSegment"), "UNLIMITED"), Ref.keyword("ERRORS", optional=True)). Sequence matches its elements in the order given, so the REJECT keyword must come immediately before LIMIT. OneOf then requires exactly one alternative after LIMIT: either a numeric literal or UNLIMITED. The trailing ERRORS keyword is optional.

_has_value_table_function (called from get_aliases_from_select) checks whether a table expression contains a function whose name is in the dialect's "value_table_functions" set. If it does, the alias goes into the standalone/value-table-function aliases. Otherwise it is treated as a regular table alias.

StatementSegment.match_grammar is a OneOf(...) of all statement-type Refs; OneOf resolves ambiguity via longest_match() with this priority: (1) the first total match (consumes all remaining segments or is followed by a valid terminator) is returned immediately; (2) otherwise the longest clean match; (3) otherwise the longest unclean match; (4) otherwise an empty match. Ties for longest in (2)/(3) go to the first matcher listed in the grammar. Options are pruned first and results cached.

`LT09._get_indexes` is a `@staticmethod` that only extracts data. It reads the select clause's child segments and finds the indexes of the SELECT keyword, the first newline, the first select target, the first whitespace after the newline, and any comment after SELECT. It also collects the select targets, the following FROM clause, and the whitespace before FROM. It packs all of this into the `SelectTargetsInfo` NamedTuple. It decides nothing about violations and makes no fixes.

`_eval` calls `_get_indexes`. It then chooses a path by target count and wildcard policy. A single target (or a wildcard with the "single" policy) goes to `_eval_single_select_target_element`. Multiple targets go to `_eval_multiple_select_target_elements`. Those two methods take the info tuple, decide whether the layout is a violation, and build the `LintFix` objects and the `LintResult`.

So extraction is separated from policy and fix generation. The extraction is a stateless layer, and the two evaluation methods work only from the data it returns.

The Linter is configuration-driven with dependency injection: FluffConfig resolves the dialect (via dialect_selector) into a pluggable `dialect_obj` Dialect object, which Linter.__init__ pulls out of config (`self.dialect = self.config.get("dialect_obj")`). The Lexer and Parser are built from that config and fetch their grammar (lexer matchers, root segment) from the dialect object, while rules are obtained separately via get_rulepack(config) and run on the parsed tree. The shared config object keeps dialect grammar and rule validation decoupled.

In the ANSI dialect, `DropViewStatementSegment.match_grammar` is a `Sequence` of "DROP", "VIEW", `Ref("IfExistsGrammar", optional=True)`, `Ref("TableReferenceSegment")` and `Ref("DropBehaviorGrammar", optional=True)`. IF EXISTS and the drop behavior (CASCADE or RESTRICT) are both optional, so each can be left out. Other dialects inherit this unless they override it. ClickHouse, Exasol, Postgres and T-SQL define their own `DropViewStatementSegment`. I read the ANSI class only, not those four.

The Vertica SelectStatementSegment copies UnorderedSelectStatementSegment.match_grammar with `insert=[OrderBy, Fetch, Limit, Ref("TimeseriesClauseSegment", optional=True), NamedWindow]`, and passes `replace_terminators=True` with a fresh terminators list (only SetOperatorSegment, WithNoSchemaBindingClauseSegment, WithDataClauseSegment). This overwrites the inherited terminators, which in the unordered segment include TimeseriesClauseSegment (plus OrderBy and Limit). That way TimeseriesClauseSegment is no longer a terminator and can be matched as an optional element in the select's sequence.

There is no special error handling: ReplaceClauseSegment.match_grammar is just Sequence("REPLACE", Bracketed(Delimited(Sequence(<expression>, "AS", Ref("SingleIdentifierGrammar"))))). BigQuery uses BaseExpressionElementGrammar for the expression part; Snowflake (dialect_snowflake.py:1983) uses ExpressionSegment. If any delimited item doesn't match expression AS identifier, the Delimited/Bracketed/Sequence match fails, so the REPLACE clause doesn't match and the text is left as an unparsable segment, which is reported as a parse error. This is the parser's default failure behaviour, which I haven't traced through its internals.

get_config_info() doesn't import any rule package's config directly. It asks the pluggy plugin manager to call `hook.get_configs_info()`. The function then merges those dicts into one mapping. The core framework only knows the hook spec. Each rule package registers its config by implementing the hook, so the core never imports rule packages for their config. New or third-party packages can add config info just by being installed.

The function is `JinjaTemplater._extract_libraries_from_config`. It reads `library_path` from config, walks it with `pkgutil.walk_packages`, and runs `spec.loader.exec_module(module)` on every module it finds. It also writes each module into `sys.modules`. A config or in-file setting can therefore run arbitrary Python at lint time, and the module name is not checked.

I did not find any tests or other callers, so the redesign below is a proposal based on this function and on `docs/source/production/security.rst`. It does not describe code that exists yet.

1. **Make loading opt-in and off by default.** Only import anything when the invoking application has explicitly enabled it, through an override or the `--library-path` CLI option. Config files and in-file config (`-- sqlfluff:...`) should not be able to turn it on. This matches the security doc's tiers: users who can edit SQL files can already edit most config through in-file config, so the guard has to sit at the point of invocation.
2. **Restrict where modules can come from.** The path should be an absolute, resolved path (`realpath`) that sits inside an allow-list of trusted roots set by the invoker. Reject `..` segments, symlink escapes and paths outside those roots. The current `os.path.join(library_path, "..")` step is a risk here, because it walks one level above the given path.
3. **Stop polluting global state.** Do not assign into `sys.modules` with bare, unprefixed names. A name like `json` could shadow a real module. Use a namespaced name or don't register the module at all.
4. **Isolate and fail safely.** If dynamic execution is still needed, run the import in a separate restricted process or sandbox. Check the module name before exec. Catch and report errors as `SQLTemplaterError`, and don't use bare `assert` for validation.
5. **Prefer a declarative alternative.** Offer an explicit allow-list of named, pre-installed modules or plugins, loaded through the existing plugin mechanism. Users would then select trusted modules by name instead of pointing at arbitrary directories.

`DepthMap.from_raws_and_root` calls `root_segment.path_to(raw)` separately for every raw segment. That repeats a tree walk each time and doesn't use any cache. To refactor it, build the map from the root's cached `raw_segments_with_ancestors`, which is what `from_parent` does. That gives a single cached traversal of the root.

Then keep only the entries for the requested raws, for example by matching on `raw.uuid`. Use `path_to` only as a fallback for a raw that isn't in the cached data. In effect, `from_raws_and_root` would delegate to the `from_parent` logic and filter the result.

`SQLLintError` in `sqlfluff/src/sqlfluff/core/errors.py` handles its `LintFix` list (`self.fixes`) in three ways:

- **State preservation.** `__reduce__` passes `self.fixes` back into the constructor when the error is pickled, so the edits survive.
- **Dictionary conversion.** `to_dict()` starts from the base dict and adds `fixes=[fix.to_dict() for fix in self.fixes]`, plus the segment position.
  - Optional-field promotion: if the error has no `end_line_pos` and there is exactly one fix, the error borrows the fix's optional position fields.
  - It only does this when the fix's `start_line_no` and `start_line_pos` match the error's.
  - The fields copied are `start_file_pos`, `end_line_no`, `end_line_pos` and `end_file_pos`.
- **Duplicate detection.** `source_signature()` returns a hashable tuple of these parts:
  - `check_tuple()`, which is the rule code and line position;
  - the description;
  - the raw strings of each fix's edit segments (the templated-file edits);
  - for every edit's `source_fixes`, a tuple of the edit text and its `source_slice` start and stop (the original-file edits).
  - The templated slice is deliberately left out of that last part, because it differs between iterations of a loop.

  Two errors count as duplicates only if both the templated and the source edits match.

The core logic is in `SQLLintError.source_signature`. The fix hoisting in `to_dict` is at lines 312–330.

SelectTargetsInfo is built by _get_indexes on every _eval call (once per select_clause). Each construction eagerly computes all fields, which means many full scans over the clause's children and its following siblings (select/newline/comment/whitespace searches, find calls, the from_clause lookup, and a list copy of pre-from whitespace). Repeating that for every select clause adds up to significant overhead, and it is paid even when the rule doesn't need all the fields. I didn't profile it.

Its override therefore sets allow_gaps=True, and the comment says this is also kept explicit to make the difference from the ANSI class clear.

DropSearchIndexStatementSegment is a BigQuery-only BaseSegment. Its `match_grammar` is a Sequence: DROP SEARCH INDEX, an optional IfExistsGrammar, an IndexReferenceSegment, ON, and a TableReferenceSegment. The BigQuery dialect registers it in its statement list through `Ref("DropSearchIndexStatementSegment")` at line 655. Because of that registration, the parser can recognise `DROP SEARCH INDEX [IF EXISTS] idx ON table` as a `drop_search_index_statement` node. The ANSI base dialect has no such statement, so it wouldn't parse this syntax. The segment's `type` is "drop_search_index_statement", which gives the parse tree a typed node that rules and the dialect fixtures can use. Any statement that doesn't fit the grammar fails to match, which is how validation happens.

In BaseSegment.recursive_crawl, the check `if not self.descendant_type_set.intersection(seg_type): return None` uses a cached set of all descendant types. If none of the requested types appear anywhere below the current segment, the method returns right away and does not iterate over or recurse into its children. A whole irrelevant branch is therefore skipped with one cheap set intersection. Without this check, the crawl would visit every node in that branch, so deeply nested irrelevant subtrees would cost time proportional to their size. With it, the cost stays small because irrelevant branches are pruned at their root.

OperatorClassReferenceSegment subclasses ansi.ObjectReferenceSegment and sets type = "operator_class_reference". It inherits the ANSI dotted-identifier reference parsing, including schema qualification. The distinct type name lets the Postgres grammar for index columns and exclusion constraints refer to operator classes explicitly. Parsed operator classes are therefore tagged as their own kind of reference in the dialect's segment type system. Rules and tooling can then handle them separately from table or column references.

dispatch_dialect_warning builds the message with format_dialect_warning, which applies the CLI's colour and format styling. It then passes the result to _dispatch instead of writing it directly. _dispatch is the single output-routing point: it writes to the configured output stream and drops empty messages when filtering is on. It is also the designated hook for subclasses to override. Using it means warnings are formatted and sent to the same place as all other CLI output.

The `StructTypeSegment` class is defined at `dialect_ansi.py:901` and overridden per dialect. Each dialect's `match_grammar` for it is a single shared object, stored once in the dialect and reached through `Ref("StructTypeSegment")`. `Ref` looks the grammar up by name at parse time (`dialect.ref`) and reuses that one object. Calling `StructTypeSegment()` at each nesting level would instead build a new segment object and a new grammar tree for each level. Deeply nested struct types would then allocate many short-lived objects, which adds memory churn and garbage-collection work. Reusing the shared grammar through `Ref` avoids that allocation.

In `Rule_JJ01._get_whitespace_ends`, the opening-marker boundary is set in the leading-modifier check. `pre` starts as the first two characters. The trailing side is handled the same way, widening `post` to `s[-3:]`.

After that come "DO" and Ref("ForInStatementsSegment"), which is the loop body, between Indent and Dedent. It ends with "END" and "FOR".

`ParsedVariant` is an immutable NamedTuple that holds the result of parsing one TemplatedFile. It has four fields: `templated_file`, `tree: Optional[BaseSegment]`, `lexing_violations` and `parsing_violations`. `tree` is None when parsing hits an unrecoverable violation. Lexing and parsing errors are kept in two separate lists instead of being raised. The `violations()` method joins the two lists, so callers can still report errors when there is no tree. `ParsedString` sits one level above it. It holds a list of `ParsedVariant`s, which is empty if templating or parsing failed, plus `templating_violations`, `time_dict`, `config`, `fname` and `source_str`. Each pipeline stage (templating, lexing, parsing) therefore records its failures in its own field, and the Optional tree lets processing continue without a parse tree.

BigQuery's MergeInsertClauseSegment is a OneOf with two alternatives. `INSERT ROW` (Sequence("INSERT","ROW")) is the wildcard-like form: it inserts the entire source row, with no column list and no VALUES clause. The other alternative is explicit insertion: INSERT, then an optional bracketed column list, then an optional ValuesClauseSegment, where the columns and values are named explicitly. There is no literal `*` wildcard in the grammar, and `INSERT ROW` is the BigQuery-specific addition over ANSI.

`_validate_dialect_specific_statements` parses the raw SQL with a `Linter` for the given dialect. It asserts there are no violations and that "unparsable" is not in the tree's `type_set()`. It then calls `parsed.tree.recursive_crawl(segment_cls.type)` to collect every segment of the expected type at any depth. It asserts that the number of those segments equals `stmt_count`. Finally, it asserts that each collected segment is an `isinstance` of `segment_cls`.

The dialect subclasses only add or change a few things relative to the ANSI grammar. Examples are Postgres adding an optional INTO clause before FROM and extra terminators, and BigQuery adding QUALIFY before OVERLAPS and a pipe-operator terminator. The ANSI `UnorderedSelectStatementSegment.match_grammar` is a Sequence of optional clauses with its own terminators and GREEDY_ONCE_STARTED parse mode. Calling `.copy(insert=[...], before=..., terminators=[...])` on it reuses that grammar and splices the dialect's additions in at the right position. The dialect therefore inherits the ANSI clause order, terminators and parse mode, and it picks up later ANSI changes automatically. It doesn't duplicate the whole grammar, which could drift out of sync with ANSI.

Modifying ListPartitionDefinitionSegment.match_grammar (the OneOf of Bracketed(Delimited(LiteralGrammar)) / LiteralGrammar inside VALUES IN (...)) would only affect the list partition path. RangePartitionDefinitionSegment and RangePartitionIntervalSegment have independent grammars (their own Bracketed/LiteralGrammar/QuotedLiteralSegment) and do not reference ListPartitionDefinitionSegment, so they are unaffected. The only dependent is PartitionSegment, which references Ref("ListPartitionDefinitionSegment") in its LIST branch (line 254) and would automatically pick up the new nested-bracket behavior (possible looser matching/fixture changes) with no changes needed there.

In PyClasslike.get_index_text, the code branches on `self.objtype`, which holds the directive's object type (class, exception, and so on). For 'class', it calls gettext `_()` with a translatable format string. The string is "%s (built-in class)" when there is no modname. Otherwise it is "%s (class in %s)", filled with the name and module. For 'exception', it skips translation and returns the bare name. Any other type returns an empty string, so no index entry is made. So the objtype check chooses which msgid goes through the translation catalog. Class entries are therefore localized and differ by module context. Exception entries are just the plain name.

When `:file:` is an absolute path (starts with `/` or `os.sep`) and doesn't exist on disk, it builds `abspath = env.srcdir / option[1:]`. ASTParenAttribute.__eq__ first uses a guard clause: `if not isinstance(other, ASTParenAttribute): return NotImplemented`. ASTBinOpExpr._stringify(transform) starts with transform(self.exprs[0]). For each remaining expression it appends ' ', the operator from self.ops[i-1], ' ', and transform(self.exprs[i]). It then joins everything with ''.join, which gives "expr op expr op expr ...".

`_consume_to_end` loops `while self._lines:`. `self._lines` is the `Deque`, whose truthiness is the deque's own length. Each pass it calls `self._lines.next()`, and `next()` calls `popleft()`. The loop appends each popped line to a local list and returns that list. Every line is removed from the deque as it is read, so the deque ends up empty and the iterator state stays consistent. The loop stops exactly when the deque is empty. `next()` raises `StopIteration` only if the deque is empty when called, and the loop guard prevents that.

Autodoc's `filter_members` method decides this member by member. It skips private members, special `__methods__` and undocumented members unless the matching options are set (`private-members`, `special-members`, `undoc-members`). It also skips anything listed in `exclude-members`, mocked objects, inherited members filtered by `inherited-members`, and members forcibly marked as skipped (`ObjectMember.skipped`). Last, it emits the `autodoc-skip-member` event, and a handler can override the decision. Sphinx uses `emit_firstresult`, so the first handler that returns a non-None value wins. If an exception occurs, the member is not kept.

The SHA-1 hash of the full URI makes a unique parent directory for each remote image. Two different URLs that end in the same filename (for example `a.com/logo.png` and `b.com/logo.png`) therefore don't overwrite each other. The sanitized basename keeps a recognizable filename and the original extension, which the image pipeline needs to identify the file type. Sanitizing (and hashing the name when it is empty or too long) keeps the name valid on disk. The per-URI path is also stable, so a re-download can reuse the existing file and send `If-Modified-Since` for a conditional request.

ASTParenExpr.__eq__ returns NotImplemented (not False) for objects that aren't ASTParenExpr. This follows Python's binary-operator protocol. NotImplemented tells Python that this class doesn't know how to compare with that type. Python then tries the reflected `other.__eq__(self)`, so the other operand can handle the comparison. If neither side handles it, Python falls back to identity comparison and the result is False. Returning False directly would skip that step and stop the other type from deciding equality. The C++ version (sphinx/sphinx/domains/cpp/_ast.py:665) does the same thing.

PythonDomain.find_obj tries candidate names in a fixed order of decreasing specificity/priority, so absolute and relative references both resolve without ambiguity. It takes the first exact hit and stops. Default mode (searchmode 0) checks the bare name first, so a fully-qualified reference wins. It then tries classname.name, then modname.name, then modname.classname.name. This lets unqualified names resolve relative to the current class or module scope. 'mod' type refs only match exactly. Only the refspecific searchmode 1 falls back to a "fuzzy" suffix match (".name"), after exact matches have been tried. That mode can return several matches, and the exact-first order is what keeps results predictable.

ASTCharLiteral.__init__ decodes the literal and sets self.value = ord(decoded) only if the decoded string has length 1. Because the AST node can't represent a multi-character value, the exception signals "not representable" and nothing is built. The parser's literal-parsing code (cpp/_parser.py, and c/_parser.py) wraps the ASTCharLiteral construction in try/except. It catches this exception and calls self.fail('Can not handle character literal resulting in multiple decoded characters.'). That turns the condition into the parser's normal DefinitionError. A single-character literal builds the node and is returned. A multi-character literal gives a clean parse error rather than an unhandled exception or a bad AST. A separate exception type lets the parser tell this case apart from UnicodeDecodeError, which it handles with its own message.

In ASTDeclaratorParen.get_type_id (C++ domain), `next` (the declarator after the parentheses) is processed first, with the base return type id. Its result is then passed as the return type id to `inner`. In `ReturnType (inner)next`, the part after the parentheses (for example function parameters or array dimensions) binds to the return type and forms the type that the inner declarator wraps. The inner declarator, such as a pointer or reference, therefore sees everything outside the parentheses as its "return type". This gives the correct inside-out C++ declarator semantics. `require_space_after_declSpecs()` is a boolean method on the declarator AST classes, and the wrapper declarators pass the result down their `next` chain.

- **Pointer and reference wrappers** (`ASTDeclaratorPtr`, `ASTDeclaratorRef`) delegate to `self.next.require_space_after_declSpecs()`. In C, `ASTDeclaratorPtr` returns `const or volatile or restrict or len(attrs) > 0 or self.next.require_space_after_declSpecs()`. In C++ it returns only the `next` result.
- **Leaf declarators** end the recursion. The `ASTDeclaratorNameParamQual`-style leaves return `self.declId is not None`. The parameter-pack declarator returns `False`. The member-pointer declarator and the paren declarator return `True` outright.
- **Base class** `ASTDeclarator` raises `NotImplementedError`.
- **Use in `_stringify` and `describe_signature`**: the pointer and reference wrappers call `self.next.require_space_after_declSpecs()` after emitting their qualifiers or attributes, and append a space only if it returns True. Then they render `next`.
- **Top level**: `ASTType` calls `self.decl.require_space_after_declSpecs()` and adds a space after the decl-specs only if that is True and the decl-specs are non-empty.

The C++ pointer-wrapper delegation is at `sphinx/sphinx/domains/cpp/_ast.py:2833`. The C version, which also ORs in its own qualifiers, is at `sphinx/sphinx/domains/c/_ast.py:1343`.

The `no_proxy` argument is an explicit exclusion list that takes precedence over the `no_proxy` environment variable. In `should_bypass_proxies`, the environment variable is read only when the argument is None. `set_environ("no_proxy", no_proxy_arg)` also temporarily puts the argument into the environment, so that `proxy_bypass` sees it. If the URL matches the list, `get_environ_proxies` returns an empty dict `{}`, meaning no proxy is used for that URL. A non-empty dict is returned only when the URL is not bypassed, and it is the proxy mapping from `getproxies()` (environment proxies by scheme). So a non-empty result means the URL did not match the `no_proxy` override, and the environment proxies should be applied.

InvalidSchema inherits from both so that it is catchable in two ways. RequestException (itself an IOError subclass) marks it as a requests-library error. It is the base for every error raised while handling a request, and it carries the `request` and `response` attributes. Catching it handles all requests failures uniformly, including this scheme failure. ValueError marks it as a bad-argument error: the caller passed a URL whose scheme is invalid or unsupported, so the value itself is wrong. This is not a network or I/O failure. Code that treats bad input generically with `except ValueError` therefore also catches it. The class docstring says "The URL scheme provided is either invalid or unsupported." The distinction is between two checks in `guess_json_utf`, and the tests cover each separately. First, `guess_json_utf` looks at the first 4 bytes for a BOM. A UTF-32 BOM returns "utf-32", a UTF-8 BOM returns "utf-8-sig", and a UTF-16 BOM returns "utf-16". The BOM-aware names are generic, so Python's codec consumes and strips the BOM when decoding. `test_guess_by_bom` checks this: data starting with "\ufeff" encoded as utf-16-be/le or utf-32-be/le is reported as plain "utf-16" or "utf-32", not the endian-specific name. Second, if no BOM is found, it counts the null bytes in the sample and checks where they sit, because JSON starts with ASCII characters. Zero nulls gives "utf-8". Two nulls at positions 0 and 2 gives "utf-16-be", and at positions 1 and 3 gives "utf-16-le". Three nulls at the start gives "utf-32-be", and at the end gives "utf-32-le". Anything else, such as `b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"`, returns None, which `test_bad_utf_like_encoding` checks. `test_encoded` round-trips `"{}"` through each encoding, covering both paths. The BOM check runs first, so BOM-bearing data is never judged by null patterns.

TestRequests (tests/test_requests.py:82) imports a set of exception types from requests.exceptions (lines 33-49: ChunkedEncodingError, ConnectionError, ConnectTimeout, ContentDecodingError, InvalidHeader, InvalidProxyURL, InvalidSchema, InvalidURL, MissingSchema, ProxyError, ReadTimeout, RequestException, RetryError, SSLError, Timeout, TooManyRedirects, UnrewindableBodyError). It also imports HTTPAdapter, HTTPDigestAuth, and SessionRedirectMixin. Those are the components that raise or catch the exceptions.

Hierarchy (src/requests/exceptions.py):
- Everything derives from RequestException, which subclasses IOError. It carries `.request` and `.response`, and fills `request` from `response.request` when it isn't given.
- ConnectionError has the subclasses ProxyError and SSLError.
- ConnectTimeout inherits from both ConnectionError and Timeout. ReadTimeout inherits from Timeout.
- InvalidURL, MissingSchema, InvalidSchema and InvalidHeader also inherit from ValueError. InvalidProxyURL subclasses InvalidURL.
- ContentDecodingError also inherits from urllib3's HTTPError.
- TooManyRedirects, ChunkedEncodingError, RetryError and UnrewindableBodyError subclass RequestException directly.

Redirects:
- In `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` (sessions.py:185-193), `resp.content` is read inside a try block. If that raises ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError or RuntimeError, the code falls back to `resp.raw.read(decode_content=False)`.
- It then raises `TooManyRedirects(..., response=resp)` once `len(resp.history) >= max_redirects`.
- The tests `test_HTTP_302_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` and `..._WITH_PARAMS` (test_requests.py:241-265) check `e.request.url`, `e.response.url` and `len(e.response.history)`. These work because RequestException carries request and response.
- When a redirect has to resend a body, utils.rewind_body (utils.py:1082-1086) raises UnrewindableBodyError if the body can't be rewound. sessions.py:250 mentions this case in a comment.

In `RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files` (used by `PreparedRequest.prepare_body`), the preparation layer normalizes the different ways a caller can describe a file upload into one uniform multipart field. It accepts a dict or a list of pairs. Each value can be a bare file object, a 2-tuple `(filename, fileobj)`, a 3-tuple that adds a content type, or a 4-tuple that adds custom headers. For a bare file object it infers the filename with `guess_filename(v)` and falls back to the field name. It reads the content from strings, bytes, file-like objects with `.read()`, or other raw data, and skips entries whose content is `None`. It then builds a `RequestField(name, data, filename, headers)`, calls `make_multipart(content_type=...)`, and passes all fields to urllib3's `encode_multipart_formdata`. That call returns the body and the `Content-Type` header with the multipart boundary.

The `test_different_connection_pool_for_tls_settings_*` and `..._mtls_settings` tests load certificate and key files by relative path, e.g. `tests/certs/expired/{server/server.pem,server/server.key,ca/ca.crt}`, `tests/certs/valid/...` and `tests/certs/mtls/client/client.{pem,key}`. HTTPError (exceptions.py:55) subclasses RequestException, which subclasses IOError (OSError). RequestException is the common base of the library's exceptions, and it carries the `request` and `response` attributes. ConnectionError (also exceptions.py:59) is a direct subclass of RequestException, a sibling of HTTPError and not a parent or child of it. ProxyError and SSLError sit below ConnectionError. The two branches are therefore disjoint. `except HTTPError` catches only status-code errors. `except ConnectionError` catches transport failures. `except RequestException` (or IOError) catches everything.

HTTPError is raised by Response.raise_for_status() in models.py:1026, using `raise HTTPError(http_error_msg, response=self)`. This happens only for 4xx and 5xx status codes, after a response has been received. Because `response=self` is passed in, a handler can inspect `e.response.status_code`, for example to retry on 5xx or give up on 4xx. models.py:765 also catches HTTPError specifically. Connection-level failures are raised in adapters.py, which wraps urllib3 errors. They are raised as ConnectionError, SSLError and so on, and have no response. So the hierarchy lets recovery code tell the two cases apart. Catch ConnectionError and retry on network problems, catch HTTPError and handle by status code, and use RequestException as the catch-all. The urllib3 `HTTPError` is imported as BaseHTTPError and is a separate class. ContentDecodingError inherits from both RequestException and BaseHTTPError.

RequestException.__init__ pops `response` and `request` from kwargs, stores them, and — if no request was given but the response has a `request` attribute (checked via hasattr) — falls back to `response.request`. It then calls `super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)` (IOError) with the remaining args. Subclasses such as JSONDecodeError reuse this by calling InvalidJSONError.__init__ explicitly.

Both derive from RequestException, but they cover different sides of an HTTP exchange.

**UnrewindableBodyError** (`exceptions.py:135`) is about the outgoing request body. It is raised when requests has to resend a body, for example on a redirect, and can't reset it to its starting position. `rewind_body()` in `utils.py` raises it in two cases:
- The body has no `seek` method, or `_body_position` isn't an integer. That means the position wasn't recorded, as with a generator or stream. The message is "Unable to rewind request body for redirect."
- `seek()` itself raises `OSError`. The message is "An error occurred when rewinding request body for redirect."

**StreamConsumedError** (`exceptions.py:127`) is about the incoming response body. It also subclasses `TypeError`. `Response.iter_content()` in `models.py` raises it when `_content_consumed` is True and `_content` is still a bool. In other words, the raw stream was already read, the content was never cached, and the caller tries to stream it again. If the content was already cached, `iter_content` replays it from memory instead of raising.

**Summary:** UnrewindableBodyError means a request body can't be re-sent. StreamConsumedError means a response stream can't be read a second time.

PreparedRequest.prepare_headers builds a fresh CaseInsensitiveDict. It runs check_header_validity(header) on each (name, value) pair, which raises on invalid headers. It then stores each pair under to_native_string(name). Names are therefore native strings and are matched case-insensitively. A later duplicate with different casing overwrites the earlier one. The values are stored unchanged.

Removing the merge_cookies calls would stop session cookies (self.cookies) and per-request cookies from being combined into one jar. In prepare_request (sessions.py:474-476), merged_cookies is built from an empty RequestsCookieJar, then self.cookies, then the request cookies, and is passed to p.prepare(cookies=...). Without the merge, only one set would reach the Cookie header. Either the session's pre-configured cookies (for example a session or auth token) or the request-specific ones would be dropped, so the authenticated request could go out unauthenticated or incomplete. During redirects (line 241), merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies) combines cookies from the redirect response with the session cookies. Removing it would drop the session cookies from the redirected request, which would break login or auth redirects that depend on them.

links parses the Link header with parse_header_links into a list of dicts, then loops over them in order and does resolved_links[key] = link, where key = link.get("rel") or link.get("url"). Nothing checks whether the key already exists, so when several entries share the same rel, each one overwrites the one before it. Only the last entry for each rel is kept, and the earlier ones are silently dropped. The result is a dict with one link per rel, built in a single O(n) pass. Entries with no rel fall back to their url as the key. They are only dropped if their url also repeats, or if the url equals some other entry's rel. Dict insertion order follows the first time a key appears, but the value is the last one seen.

Version validation is not implemented in the exception hierarchy. The hierarchy only defines the marker class `RequestsDependencyWarning(RequestsWarning)`, which is a Warning, not an exception, and so does not break existing code. The checking is done in `requests/__init__.py` by `check_compatibility(urllib3_version, chardet_version, charset_normalizer_version)`. It parses the version strings and uses asserts to enforce these ranges: urllib3 >= 1.21.1, chardet >= 3.0.2 and < 6, and charset_normalizer >= 2.0.0 and < 4. At import time the call is wrapped in `try/except (AssertionError, ValueError)`. On a mismatch it calls `warnings.warn(..., RequestsDependencyWarning)` instead of raising, so import still succeeds. `_check_cryptography` does the same for old cryptography versions. `check_compatibility` also warns directly if neither chardet nor charset_normalizer is installed.

After the hostname check, should_strip_auth returns False (keeps the Authorization header) for an http→https redirect on the same host. This applies only when the old URL uses port 80 or none and the new URL uses port 443 or none. The code comment says this "isn't specified by RFC 7235" but is kept so older requests versions, which allowed any same-host redirect, don't break. The RFC-style principle is kept for everything else: a different host always strips auth. After the special case, the "standard case" strips auth if the port or scheme changed, apart from default-port equivalence for the same scheme. The exemption is narrow because it covers only the http→https upgrade on default ports. It is also not a downgrade, because the redirect goes to a more secure scheme.

In each loop iteration, resolve_redirects does the following:

1. **Consuming the body.** It reads `resp.content` so the socket can be released. If that raises ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError or RuntimeError, it falls back to `resp.raw.read(decode_content=False)`. It then checks `max_redirects` and calls `resp.close()` to return the connection to the pool. This happens for every redirect response, whether or not the caller passed `stream=True`.

2. **History.** It appends `resp` to a local `hist` list and sets `resp.history = hist[1:]`. That slice leaves out the original response, so history holds only the earlier redirect responses. The `max_redirects` check uses `len(resp.history)`.

3. **Rewinding the body.** The method works on a copy of the request (`req.copy()`).
   - For redirect codes other than 307 and 308, it drops Content-Length, Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding and sets the body to None.
   - For 307 and 308 the body is kept. The request counts as `rewindable` only if `_body_position` is not None and the headers include Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding. In that case it calls `rewind_body(prepared_request)` to seek the body back to its start.
   - A failed `tell()` sets `_body_position` to a bare `object()`, which is not None. That keeps `rewindable` true, so `rewind_body` raises UnrewindableBodyError instead of the connection hanging.

4. **Yielding.** With `yield_requests`, it yields the prepared request. Otherwise it sends the request with `allow_redirects=False`, reads the next redirect target, and yields the response.

The decorator at test_utils.py:566-567 is `@pytest.mark.parametrize("value, expected", (...))`. Its first argument is a string of comma-separated argument names. Pytest matches those names to the parameters of `test__parse_content_type_header(value, expected)`. The second argument is a tuple of cases, each a `(header_string, (content_type, params_dict))` pair. For every case pytest generates one test invocation. It unpacks the pair into `value` and `expected`. The body then asserts `_parse_content_type_header(value) == expected`. The cases cover plain types, charset parameters, quoted values, parameters with no `=`, and stray `;`.

In `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects`, each hop starts from a copy of the previous request (`prepared_request = req.copy()`). The copy carries its own `_cookies` jar, so the session jar isn't touched at this point. The steps for each hop are:

1. **Clear the stale header.** The loop pops the old `Cookie` header from the copied request (`headers.pop("Cookie", None)`).
2. **Extract.** `extract_cookies_to_jar(prepared_request._cookies, req, resp.raw)` pulls `Set-Cookie` cookies from the redirect response into the copy's own jar. It uses the old `req`, not the mutated copy, because the copy's URL and headers have already been changed.
3. **Merge.** `merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies)` adds the session's cookies into that per-request jar.
4. **Prepare.** `prepared_request.prepare_cookies(prepared_request._cookies)` rebuilds the `Cookie` header from the combined jar.
5. **Carry forward.** `req = prepared_request`, so the next hop copies a request whose jar already holds the cookies from earlier hops.
6. **Update the session jar.** After each `self.send(...)`, `extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, prepared_request, resp.raw)` stores the new response's cookies in the session jar. Later hops then see them when they merge. In `yield_requests` mode the loop yields the request instead of sending it, so this step doesn't run.

resolve_redirects is the driver loop. It calls get_redirect_target(resp) to get the Location, which returns None if the response is not a redirect. The Location is decoded from latin1 to UTF-8. On each hop, resolve_redirects copies the previous request and resolves the new URL (scheme-relative, relative, fragment handling). It then calls rebuild_method, drops the Cookie header and re-merges cookies from the jar, calls rebuild_proxies, and then calls rebuild_auth(prepared_request, resp). rebuild_auth compares response.request.url (the old URL) with the new prepared_request.url using should_strip_auth. should_strip_auth returns True if the hostname differs, or if the scheme or port changes. The exceptions are an http→https upgrade on the default ports and matching default ports. When it returns True, rebuild_auth deletes the Authorization header. It then re-applies .netrc credentials for the new URL if trust_env is set, so credentials are never leaked to a different host. After the request is sent with allow_redirects=False, get_redirect_target is called on the new response to decide whether the loop continues. The loop is capped by max_redirects.

register_hook flattens an iterable: it extends self.hooks[event] with each callable item, so the iterable itself is never stored. deregister_hook calls self.hooks[event].remove(hook), which matches by equality against the stored items. If you pass the same iterable you registered, remove() looks for the list or tuple itself, raises ValueError, and the method returns False. The hooks stay registered. Removal only works one callable at a time. The two methods are therefore asymmetric, and a bulk registration can't be undone with a single call. Non-callable items in the iterable are also dropped silently at registration.

Response keeps two separate pieces of state. `_content` holds the cached bytes. Its sentinel is `False`, meaning "not read yet". `_content_consumed` records whether the stream was read. Neither lives in the pickle logic.

**Lazy materialization.** The `content` property (models.py:891-907) only reads when `_content is False`. It then joins the `iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)` chunks into `_content` and sets `_content_consumed = True`. `iter_content` (models.py:839-850) keeps streaming and caching apart. If `_content_consumed` is false, it yields live chunks from `raw`. Otherwise it replays the cached `_content` through `iter_slices`. If the stream was consumed but `_content` is still the `False` sentinel, it raises `StreamConsumedError`.

**Serialization.** `__attrs__` (models.py:645) lists the picklable fields. It includes `_content` but leaves out `raw` and `_content_consumed`. `__getstate__` (models.py:711-717) first reads `self.content` if the stream hasn't been consumed, so the whole body is buffered. It then returns only the `__attrs__` fields. `__setstate__` (models.py:719-725) restores those fields, sets `_content_consumed = True` and sets `raw = None`. An unpickled Response therefore replays its cached bytes and never touches a live socket.

Pickling a streamed response forces its content to be read in full. Streaming behaviour is otherwise unchanged.

Response keeps two pieces of state: `_content`, which starts as `False` meaning "not read yet", and `_content_consumed`, which starts as `False`. `iter_content()` has two paths. If the content hasn't been consumed, it returns the `generate()` generator, which reads lazily from `raw` in `chunk_size` pieces, so a large body is never fully in memory. That generator sets `_content_consumed = True` when it finishes. If the content was already consumed and `_content` holds real bytes, `iter_content()` instead returns `iter_slices(self._content, chunk_size)`, which replays the cached bytes. If it was consumed through streaming and `_content` is still `False`, it raises `StreamConsumedError`. The `content` property reads the whole body once with `b"".join(self.iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE))` and caches it in `_content`. It raises `RuntimeError` if the stream was already consumed without being cached. It then sets `_content_consumed = True`.

`Response.__enter__` returns self, and `__exit__` always calls `self.close()`. `close()` closes the raw urllib3 response (`self.raw.close()`) only when `_content_consumed` is false, meaning the body wasn't fully read. Then, if `raw` has a `release_conn` attribute, it calls `release_conn()` to return the connection to the pool. When the content was already consumed, the raw close is skipped, because the stream has already been read to the end and closed. `release_conn` is looked up with `getattr(..., None)`, so raw objects without it still work. As far as I can tell, `release_conn` is also safe to call more than once in urllib3, so repeated calls to `close()` or the context manager exit don't fail. That last point is from my knowledge of urllib3, not from this repo. The repo has no flag of its own that blocks a second `close()`.

The order is a dependency chain. prepare_auth runs after prepare_body (and the method, URL, headers and cookies steps) because auth schemes such as OAuth sign the fully prepared request, including its body and headers. prepare_auth also calls `auth(self)` and then recomputes Content-Length from the body, which only makes sense once the body exists. prepare_hooks runs after prepare_auth because authenticators can register hooks while they run. Those hooks have to be present when the hooks are prepared, so hooks come last. Running the steps in parallel or in another order would make auth sign an incomplete request, or would miss hooks that auth adds.

In TLSServer.__init__ (requests/tests/testserver/server.py), SSL setup is inline. It creates ssl.SSLContext(PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER) and calls load_cert_chain(cert_chain, keyfile). If mutual_tls is set, it sets verify_mode = CERT_OPTIONAL and calls load_verify_locations(cacert). No SSLContextBuilder exists in the codebase, so what follows is a proposal.

Refactor: split the constructor logic into two private steps, or two builder methods:
- `with_cert_chain(cert, key)` handles identity loading only, via load_cert_chain.
- `with_mutual_tls(cacert, mode=CERT_OPTIONAL)` handles verification only. It sets verify_mode and calls load_verify_locations.
- `build()` returns the ssl.SSLContext.

TLSServer would then accept a prebuilt context, or call the builder, and keep only the socket wrapping in `_create_socket_and_bind`.

Architectural implications:
- Benefits:
  - Each piece has a single responsibility.
  - The verify mode becomes configurable (CERT_REQUIRED vs CERT_OPTIONAL).
  - The client-CA assumption can be separated from the server cert, so the CA need not be the same one that issued the server certificate.
  - The context can be tested and reused without starting a server thread.
  - Dependency injection becomes possible.
  - Failures from bad certificates surface at build time.
- Costs:
  - It adds one more component to maintain, which is arguably over-engineering for a small test server.
  - Constructor signatures change (cert_chain, keyfile, mutual_tls and cacert would be replaced by a context or builder).
  - Existing tests that construct TLSServer would need updating.
  - Ordering rules need to be documented, because the context must be fully built before wrap_socket.

`_body_position` has three states because a boolean can't separate "not a stream" from "stream whose position couldn't be recorded". 
- `None` (set in `__init__`, models.py:349) means there is no seekable-style stream body, so nothing needs rewinding. This covers a plain string, dict or no body. On a redirect, `rewindable` is False and the body is simply resent.
- An integer is the result of `body.tell()` (models.py:537). It is the offset to `seek()` back to on a redirect, so the value itself is needed. A boolean would lose it.
- A sentinel `object()` is stored when `tell()` raises `OSError` (models.py:541). The comment says this "differentiates from None, allowing us to catch a failed `tell()` later". It is not None, so `sessions.py:251` treats the body as needing a rewind. `rewind_body` (utils.py:1076) then fails the `isinstance(..., integer_types)` check and raises `UnrewindableBodyError`. Without the sentinel, a failed `tell()` would look like "no stream". The redirect would resend a partly consumed stream, and the connection could hang because of the Content-Length mismatch (sessions.py:248-250).

A boolean `can_rewind` would only give "rewindable / not rewindable". It couldn't carry the offset, and it couldn't separate "nothing to rewind, carry on" from "should rewind but can't, so raise an error".

Each __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__ calls key.lower(). Strings are immutable, but str.lower() allocates a brand-new string on every call. The call is also a Python-level method call, and the new string must be hashed again before the OrderedDict lookup, because the hash of the new string isn't cached. In a high-frequency lookup loop over large data this adds up to a lot of allocation, hashing and garbage-collection work, even when the same keys are looked up again and again. The cost is paid on every access, and on top of the real dict lookup. Optimization: normalize each key once and reuse the result. Options are a bounded memoization cache for key→lowered key (functools.lru_cache on a static helper, or a small dict cache), or interning the lowered keys. Callers can also pre-lowercase keys, or use lower_items() / the internal _store directly in hot paths. Another option is to skip lower() when the key is already lowercase, for example by checking a cached flag. Keep the cache bounded to avoid unbounded memory growth.

Because a streamed body (file object, generator, or iterator) is sent as-is, either with a Content-Length or with chunked transfer encoding, and is never read into memory. A multipart request must be built by `_encode_files(files, data)`. That function needs the data as key/value fields, so it can put each one in its own multipart part. It also needs the full body in memory so it can compute the boundaries and the Content-Length. A stream is opaque and may be unbounded, so it can't be split into fields, and merging it would mean reading all of it and defeating the streaming. The code therefore refuses the combination and raises `NotImplementedError("Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive.")`. The stated reason is my reading of the code. I found no comment that explains it.

guess_filename only accepts the object's `name` if it is a non-empty string (isinstance basestring) and isn't a pseudo-name wrapped in angle brackets like "<stdin>" or "<fdopen>". It then returns os.path.basename(name), which strips directory components. So the multipart upload doesn't send the client's local directory structure or path-traversal pieces (e.g. "../../etc/passwd"). It also avoids non-string names, such as an integer fd, and avoids leaking meaningless pseudo-file names. Stripping the path is the main security effect. The bracket and type checks are robustness and sanity checks, not full security validation.

The function checks `morsel["max-age"]` first because `http.cookiejar.Cookie` only stores an absolute `expires` timestamp (epoch seconds). It has no field for a relative lifetime. Max-age is a relative number of seconds, so it has to be converted. Max-age also takes precedence over `expires`, which matches the HTTP cookie rules. If max-age is set, the function computes `expires = int(time.time() + int(max-age))`, which is the current epoch time plus the max-age seconds. If max-age isn't an integer, the `int()` call raises ValueError, and the function re-raises it as a TypeError ("max-age: ... must be integer"). If there is no max-age but `expires` is set, the function parses that date string with `time.strptime` using the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT". It then converts the result to epoch seconds with `calendar.timegm`. The resulting `expires` value is passed to `create_cookie`.

BaseAdapter implicitly inherits only from `object`, so `super().__init__()` just calls `object.__init__()` and does nothing at the moment. It is a cooperative-inheritance (MRO-friendly) pattern. If a subclass mixes BaseAdapter with other classes, or BaseAdapter later gets a parent class, the initialization chain still reaches every `__init__` in the MRO. This keeps the adapter framework extensible without changing the base. The code has no comment stating this, so the reasoning is inferred from the code.

Each MockRequest does urlparse(self._r.url) in __init__ (scheme), in get_host (netloc; also called via get_origin_req_host and the `host`/`origin_req_host` properties), and in get_full_url when a Host header is set. CookieJar calls these methods several times per request (add_cookie_header, extract_cookies, policy checks such as domain/return_ok, request_host, etc.), so the same unchanging URL is re-parsed over and over. urlparse does string splitting, validation and tuple building, and it is only partly cached. At high volume this adds up to wasted CPU and allocations. Optimization: parse once, in __init__, and store the result, e.g. `self._parsed = urlparse(request.url)`. Then set `self.type = self._parsed.scheme`, have get_host return `self._parsed.netloc`, and have get_full_url reuse `self._parsed` in urlunparse (or cache the computed full URL). Optionally use functools.cached_property for lazy parsing. This keeps the wrapped request read-only, because the parsed result is an immutable named tuple held on the wrapper and the request is never modified. Since the request URL is not changed during the cookie operation, the cache stays valid. New headers still go only into _new_headers. If the URL could change, create a fresh MockRequest per operation, which is how it is already used.

`host` is a property (a descriptor call) that calls `get_host()`, which runs `urlparse(self._r.url).netloc` on every access. That costs two Python-level calls, and the parse is the expensive part. `urlparse` does URL splitting, string scanning and building a ParseResult namedtuple, and nothing is cached on the instance. The call overhead is small (the property lookup plus one extra frame). Over millions of iterations the repeated urlparse dominates, and the cost grows linearly because the same URL is re-parsed each time. Direct attribute access would just be a dict lookup.

Optimization: compute the host once and memoize it. For example, set `self._host = urlparse(url).netloc` in `__init__` (the way `self.type` is already stored), or use `functools.cached_property` on `host`, or cache the result lazily in `get_host`. Have `get_origin_req_host` and `host` return the cached value. The memoized value must be invalidated, or the URL treated as immutable, if `self._r.url` can change. Here the request is documented as read-only, so caching is safe. Another option is `functools.lru_cache` on the URL-to-netloc parse.

ConnectionError is a direct subclass of RequestException (distinct from HTTPError, Timeout, etc.) that marks failures to reach/talk to the server at the network level (DNS, refused/closed connections, protocol errors, exhausted retries) rather than HTTP-level or other request errors. HTTPAdapter.send translates urllib3's ProtocolError/OSError/MaxRetryError/ClosedPoolError into it, so callers can catch it specifically. It also acts as a base for more specific failures: ProxyError, SSLError, and ConnectTimeout.

HTTPAdapter.send() in adapters.py translates urllib3's ProxyError into requests' ProxyError. This happens either when a MaxRetryError has a _ProxyError as its reason (line 670-671), or when a bare _ProxyError is caught (line 682-683). requests.exceptions.ProxyError subclasses ConnectionError, which subclasses RequestException. So callers that catch ConnectionError or RequestException also catch it.

The test checks that when a POST with a generator body (so it gets `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and a body) gets a 302, `resolve_redirects` turns it into a body-less GET. That GET must not keep the headers that describe the old body. The code in `sessions.py` purges `Content-Length`, `Content-Type` and `Transfer-Encoding` and sets `body = None`. This applies to every redirect status except 307 and 308. Those two keep the method and body, so the headers are kept too. The test is a regression test for psf/requests issue #3490, where `Transfer-Encoding` was left on the redirected request. HISTORY.md:814 records the fix. I inferred the consequences below from how HTTP works. The code and tests don't state them.

If the headers stayed on the GET:
- **Protocol breakage:** `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` tells the server to expect a chunked body, but none is sent. The server could hang waiting for chunks or reject the request as malformed. The connection could also desync.
- **Request smuggling or desync:** a mismatch between the framing headers and the actual body is the classic cause of request smuggling. Leftover `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` on a bodiless request leaves an intermediary and the origin able to disagree about where the request ends.
- **Stale metadata:** `Content-Type` would claim a payload that isn't there. Servers or proxies might then try to parse a nonexistent body, or leak details of the original POST payload to the redirect target.
- **Rewind logic:** the `rewindable` check in `sessions.py` uses the presence of `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` to decide whether to rewind the body. Leftover headers could trigger pointless rewinds or errors.

Every operation (__getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__) calls key.lower() on the key before the OrderedDict lookup. That allocates a new lowercase string each time and adds a Python-level method call. Nothing caches the lowered key. The lookup is still O(1), but the per-call overhead (a string allocation, plus the Python dispatch through MutableMapping) is paid on every access. With thousands of header lookups per request, that overhead adds up. Other costs: the store is an OrderedDict holding (key, value) tuples, so reads need an extra [1] index. __eq__ and copy rebuild whole CaseInsensitiveDict objects, which re-lowers every key.

TestTestServer (requests/tests/test_testserver.py) imports `Server` from `tests.testserver.server`. The class is in requests/tests/testserver/server.py and subclasses `threading.Thread`.

**Context manager protocol:**
- `__enter__` (line 117) calls `start()`, which runs `run()` in a new thread. `run()` creates the socket, binds it and listens. If `port=0`, it reads back the OS-assigned port, then sets `ready_event` and calls `_handle_requests()`.
- `__enter__` blocks on `ready_event.wait(5)` and raises `RuntimeError` on timeout. It then returns `(host, port)`, which is why the tests write `with Server(...) as (host, port)`.
- `_handle_requests` loops `requests_to_handle` times. Each pass does a `select`-guarded accept, runs the handler on the connection, appends the result to `handler_results`, and closes the client socket.
- If `wait_to_close_event` is set, `run()` then waits on it for up to 5 seconds. A `finally` block always sets `ready_event`, closes the server socket (ignoring `OSError`), and sets `stop_event`.
- `__exit__` (line 123) behaves differently depending on whether the block raised. With no exception, it waits on `stop_event` so the handler can finish. With an exception, it sets `wait_to_close_event` so the thread doesn't sit out its timeout. In both cases it closes the server socket to unblock any pending accept, calls `join()`, and returns `False` so exceptions propagate.

**How the tests exercise this:**
- `test_basic` checks that the handler and client exchange messages inside the `with` block.
- `test_server_closes` connects after the block exits and expects `socket.error`, because the listening socket was closed and the thread joined.
- `test_basic_waiting_server` passes a `wait_to_close_event`. The server thread stays alive until the test sets the event.
- `test_multiple_requests` sets `requests_to_handle=5`. The sixth request raises `ConnectionError`, because the server has stopped accepting after five.
- `test_requests_after_timeout_are_not_received` reads `handler_results` after the `with` block. That is safe because `__exit__` has already joined the thread.

`fill_value` is the value substituted wherever the indexer holds -1. In `_getitem_with_mask`, -1 is a "missing" sentinel and does not mean "last element". The default is `dtypes.NA`, which `dtypes.get_fill_value(self.dtype)` resolves to the dtype's natural missing value. For floats that is NaN, and other dtypes may be promoted so they can hold NaN. A mask is built from the -1 positions, and `where(~mask, data, fill_value)` overwrites those positions. That also holds for size-zero arrays, where the result is `broadcast_to(fill_value, mask.shape)`.

The tests in `VariableSubclassobjects` show the effect. With the default, `[0, -1, 1]` on `[0, 1, 2]` gives `[0, nan, 1]`. With `fill_value=-99` it gives `[0, -99, 1]`. In the nd-indexer test, `fill_value=-1` returns the indexer itself.

Changing `fill_value` only changes what is written at the masked positions. Negative indices are still treated as masked and are not wrapped around. The code has a TODO to check that all other integers are non-negative.

`expected_dtype` picks how `_assertIndexedLikeNDArray` checks the type of the indexed element. It has three modes:

- **`None` (default):** The helper compares Python/numpy types, not dtypes. It asserts `type(variable.values[0]) is type(expected_value0)` and `type(variable[0].values) is type(expected_value0)`. The tests use this where the scalar's type matters more than a dtype. One case is a datetime built from a Python `datetime`, where the result should be an `np.datetime64` scalar. The other is NaT, where the helper compares scalar types and skips the dtype.
- **A specific dtype (e.g. `np.int32`, `float`, `np.dtype("U3")`, `"datetime64[us]"`, `"timedelta64[ns]"`):** The helper asserts that `variable.values[0].dtype` and `variable[0].values.dtype` both equal that dtype. This checks that indexing preserves the exact dtype, including the datetime/timedelta unit (`us` vs `ns`). It is used for ints, floats, strings, and datetime/timedelta64.
- **`False`:** The helper skips type and dtype checking entirely. Only the shape, identity and value checks run. `test_index_0d_object` uses this for arbitrary Python objects held in an object array. There the element is the original object, so it has no numpy dtype to compare, and `None` would also be wrong.

The `elif expected_dtype is not False` branch is what separates "no dtype given, compare types" from "explicitly skip the check".

It handles NaNs by masking all-NA slices and restoring them with `fill_value`. It runs the supplied `func` (argmin or argmax) and maps the resulting indices to coordinate labels. That mapping works for both chunked (dask) and non-chunked arrays. It then renames the result to `dim` and copies attrs. Passing `func` in lets the same helper serve both idxmin and idxmax, so the method only decides which reduction to use and the helper does everything else.

The tests in TestGetItem don't depend on each other. Each one builds its own tree, and there is no shared fixture or ordering. The dependency they share is on `DataTree.from_dict`. They pass a path like "/results/highres" and expect `from_dict` to create the intermediate "results" node, through `_set_item(..., new_nodes_along_path=True)`. Only then can `__getitem__` resolve "results", "results/highres" and "results/highres/temp".

The correctness of those three tests therefore rests on four behaviours of `from_dict`:
- It builds the intermediate nodes along each path.
- It sorts the paths by depth, so parents are created before children.
- It copies the DataTree and Dataset values it is given.
- It names the root with the `name` argument, as in `name="folder1"`.

If `from_dict` breaks, those tests fail even though `__getitem__` is fine. The remaining tests (self access, single and missing variable access) build their trees with the `DataTree(...)` constructor directly. They don't use `from_dict`, so they check variable access without it.

It also uses `assert_identical` from `xarray.testing`. The DataTree class under test comes from `xarray.core.datatree`.

Constraints on verifying equivalence:
- `assert_identical` is the only equivalence check. It is used just for the data-variable lookups: `results["temp"]` and `folder1["results/highres/temp"]` against `data["temp"]`. It compares values, dims, coords, name and attrs, so the check is strict. It can only compare a DataArray taken from the tree with one taken from a plain `xr.Dataset`.
- The node tests do not use `assert_identical`. They only check `.name` and object identity (`dt["."] is dt`).
- Whole-tree equivalence, such as a subtree or a multi-variable selection, is not checked. Two tests are marked xfail: `results[["temp","p"]]` and `results[{"temp": 1}]`. Both are expected to fail, because indexing with a list or dict doesn't work on a DataTree yet.

The test builds two dask-backed variables on the same dims (lat, lon) with different dask chunking: x is (50,100) and y is (100,50). A dask array's chunks are per-array and distributed, but an h5netcdf/HDF5 file stores chunking per variable on disk. The test therefore sets `encoding["chunksizes"]` (plus `original_shape`) explicitly on each variable. That is how the writer is told what on-disk chunk layout to use for each variable, so it doesn't have to infer one from dask's chunks, which are inconsistent between the two variables. After the roundtrip, it asserts that each variable's `chunksizes` encoding survives: x stays (50,100) and y stays (100,50).

There is no special conflict-resolution code: DatasetArithmetic(ImplementsDatasetReduce, SupportsArithmetic, DatasetOpsMixin) relies on plain Python MRO (left-to-right base order) and the bases have disjoint responsibilities (reduce-method factory / __array_ufunc__ / generated operator dunders, all with __slots__ = ()). __array_priority__ = 50 on DatasetArithmetic doesn't arbitrate between the mixins; it makes NumPy ndarrays (priority 0) defer to xarray's binary/reflected operators (DataArray uses 60 > Variable 50 so binary ops with DataArray win).

Dataset.stack loops `result = result._stack_once(...)`, so each call rebuilds from the prior result: non-stacked variables (including earlier MultiIndex coords) are shallow-copied, indexes of stacked coords are dropped (`drop_indexes` via get_all_coords), surviving `_indexes` are kept and merged with the new stacked index (`index_cls.stack` + `create_variables`, popping old entries to keep coordinate order), and `_replace_with_new_dims(new_variables, coord_names, indexes)` returns a consistent new Dataset each iteration.

The test shows that `encoding` is metadata that travels with a Variable. It describes how the data was stored on disk, for example in a file. It is not part of the Variable's data or identity. Shape-preserving operations (T, [...], squeeze, isel with a full slice, set_dims, and both deep and shallow copy) return a Variable with `encoding` equal to the original's. The test checks the values with `assert_identical` on `to_base_variable()`, and it checks the encoding separately with `expected.encoding == actual.encoding`. So encoding is carried through these operations, but it is not part of what `assert_identical` compares. Another test, `test_drop_encoding`, shows that dropping it takes an explicit `drop_encoding()` call.

In test_concat (xarray/tests/test_variable.py:484), `Variable.concat([v, w], positions=[np.arange(0,10,2), np.arange(1,10,2)], dim="a")` has no side effects on the inputs. Variable.concat (xarray/core/variable.py:1716) builds a new Variable. It does not modify `v`, `w` or the position arrays. Attrs are merged and the encoding is copied from the first variable. The only extra work is that the concatenated result is reordered with a `take`.

How it differs from simple concatenation:
- **Simple concatenation:** with `positions=None`, the variables are joined in the order given. Here that gives [0..4, 5..9] along "a". If `dim` is not an existing dimension, it is stacked as a new axis 0.
- **With `positions`:** the data is still concatenated first, along the existing axis. Then `positions` is treated as the target index of each element: `indices = inverse_permutation(np.concatenate(positions))` and `data = take(data, indices, axis=axis)`. So `positions` says where each input's elements end up in the result, rather than the order in which the inputs are joined. The test's `positions` interleave the two inputs, so the result is [0,5,1,6,...], which equals `np.array([x, y]).ravel(order="F")`.
- **Dimension ordering:** unchanged. The dims stay the same as the first variable's, and the concatenated dimension keeps its axis. Only the order of elements along that axis changes.
- **Data layout:** `take` gives a new array with the elements permuted. This makes a copy and, for lazy dask data, adds another graph step.
- **Scope:** `positions` is only used when `dim` already exists. It is ignored on the new-dimension (stack) path.
- **Status:** the code carries the comment "TODO: deprecate this option -- we don't need it for groupby any more."

`cftime_datetime - CFTimeIndex` isn't handled by the cftime scalar's own `__sub__`. Python falls back to `CFTimeIndex.__rsub__`, which computes `other - np.array(self)`. That gives an object array of `datetime.timedelta`s, and it is wrapped in `pd.TimedeltaIndex(...)`. If the difference is too large for pandas' nanosecond-resolution Timedelta, e.g. `a.date_type(1, 1, 1) - a`, pandas raises `OutOfBoundsTimedelta` or `OverflowError`. Both are listed in `OUT_OF_BOUNDS_TIMEDELTA_ERRORS`. `__rsub__` catches them and re-raises `ValueError("The time difference exceeds the range of values that can be expressed at the nanosecond resolution.")`. The same check is in `__sub__` for index-minus-index.

The constraint behind the check is that cftime subtraction yields Python `datetime.timedelta` objects, which cover a very wide range. The result is converted to a `pd.TimedeltaIndex`, which stores int64 nanoseconds and covers only about ±292 years. A difference outside that range can't be represented, so the code raises a clear error instead of the raw pandas/overflow error.

NDArrayMixin (a subclass of NdimSizeLenMixin) delegates to a wrapped `self.array`, which the subclass must provide. Its default `dtype` property returns `self.array.dtype`. Its default `shape` property returns `self.array.shape`. Its default `__getitem__(key)` returns `self.array[key]`. `__repr__` also delegates, printing `ClassName(array=...)`. The parent mixin supplies `ndim`, `size` and `__len__`, all computed from `self.shape`. Because those are derived from `shape`, overriding `shape` also changes them. The class sets `__slots__ = ()` and its methods are annotated `self: Any`, so it adds no state of its own. A subclass sets `array` and overrides only the `dtype`, `shape` or `__getitem__` it needs to change. The docstring says this explicitly.

Each class's __eq__ is `return isinstance(other, type(self))`. type(self) is evaluated at runtime to get the instance's concrete class (AlwaysGreaterThan or AlwaysLessThan), and isinstance checks whether `other` is an instance of that class or a subclass. So an instance equals only instances of its own class (including subclasses). It never equals an instance of the other sentinel class or any other value. The two classes are independent, with no shared base, so INF != NINF. @functools.total_ordering fills in the remaining comparison methods (__le__, __ge__ and the like) from the one defined ordering method (__gt__ or __lt__) plus this __eq__. The same code appears in xarray/namedarray/dtypes.py (lines 19-20 and 28-29), where it is typed with `other: object`.

IndexVariable.__init__ keeps the parent Variable signature (dims, data, attrs, encoding, fastpath). It first calls super().__init__(...), so the parent does all the normal setup and validation. It then checks `self.ndim != 1` and raises `ValueError("IndexVariable objects must be 1-dimensional")`. The class name in the message comes from `type(self).__name__`. After the check, it eagerly wraps the data in a `PandasIndexingAdapter` if it isn't one already.

In H5NetCDFStore.__init__ (xarray/xarray/backends/h5netcdf_.py), a pre-opened h5netcdf.File or h5netcdf.Group is wrapped in a DummyFileManager. If `group` is None, `find_root_and_group(manager)` splits the object into its root File and a group path. So a Group passed in is resolved to its root plus a path, and the store re-resolves that path on each access. If `group` is given, the manager must be exactly an h5netcdf.File (`type(manager) is not h5netcdf.File` raises ValueError). The file is then used as the root and `group` is the path inside it. A Group object cannot be combined with `group`.

In both cases the store keeps only the root and a group path. `_acquire` calls `_nc4_require_group(root, self._group, self._mode, ...)` on every access, so `ds` is re-resolved each time rather than cached. With `mode=None`, which is the default for a pre-opened object, `_nc4_require_group` has no write mode to go on, so it will not create a missing group.

Possible consistency issues:
- DummyFileManager does not reopen or close the file. The caller owns the handle, so closing it elsewhere leaves the store with a stale handle.
- The group is looked up by path on each access. If the file is modified outside the store, for example the group is deleted or renamed, the lookup can fail or return different data.
- A pre-opened handle is not covered by the CachingFileManager's reopening and locking logic. Several stores sharing one handle can see each other's changes.
- `_mode` is not inferred from the object, so group creation behaviour may not match how the file was actually opened.

IndexVariable.concat (classmethod) keeps the data as pandas Index objects instead of converting them to NumPy arrays. It first checks that every input is an IndexVariable and raises TypeError if not. It takes the underlying pandas indexes (`v._data.array`) and uses `indexes[0].append(indexes[1:])`, so pandas handles the mixed index types (PeriodIndex, MultiIndex and others) and their type information is preserved. If `positions` is given, it computes `nputils.inverse_permutation(np.concatenate(positions))` and applies `data.take(indices)` to restore the original positional order. Then `maybe_coerce_to_str(data, variables)` keeps string dtypes as str, because pandas would otherwise turn them into object. Attrs are merged with `merge_attrs`. Unless `shortcut` is set, it raises ValueError("inconsistent dimensions") when dims differ. The result is `cls(first_var.dims, data, attrs)`.

DummyChunkManager subclasses the ABC ChunkManagerEntrypoint (parallelcompat.py:186). In __init__ it sets `array_cls = DummyChunkedArray`, and it overrides the abstract methods. `is_chunked_array` is an isinstance check against DummyChunkedArray. `chunks` returns `data.chunks`. `rechunk` calls `data.rechunk`. `normalize_chunks`, `from_array`, `compute` and `apply_gufunc` forward to dask (`dask.array.core.normalize_chunks`, `da.from_array`, `dask.array.compute`, `dask.array.gufunc.apply_gufunc`). Architectural implications:

Trade-offs:
- **Benefit:** xarray imports faster and works without Dask installed.
- **Benefit:** the Dask import cost is paid only if a chunk manager is actually used.

- **Cost:** a missing Dask raises `ImportError` at call time rather than at import time.
- **Cost:** static analysis and type checking are weaker, which is why the code carries `type: ignore` comments.

CopyOnWriteArray wraps a (often lazy, backend/on-disk) array and only copies it when a write happens. Opening or reading a dataset, and indexing it, therefore never loads or duplicates the data. The copy is a one-time `np.array(self.array)` in `_ensure_copied`. The `_copied` flag guards it, so it runs on the first `__setitem__`, `_oindex_set` or `_vindex_set` and not again. Writes then go to a private in-memory copy and can't change the original backing array or file. Reads (`get_duck_array`) pass straight through to the wrapped array.

Interaction with indexing: `__getitem__`, `_oindex_get` and `_vindex_get` don't copy. They index the wrapped array, which stays lazy if it is lazy, and return a new CopyOnWriteArray around the result. Indexing a CopyOnWriteArray is therefore still lazy and the copy-on-write wrapper carries over to the child. Each child has its own `_copied=False` and copies independently on its own first write. `__deepcopy__` also just re-wraps the same underlying array without copying it, because the array may point to files on disk. The wrapped array is never forced into memory except by a write.

The deep copy exists so that factorize() can mutate the grouper without changing the user's original object. For example, BinGrouper.factorize() updates BinGrouper.bins with the output of pd.cut when bins is given as an int. Without the copy, the first grouping operation would overwrite the shared grouper's bins with concrete edges computed from that data. A later grouping with the same grouper on other data would then reuse those stale bins instead of recomputing them. Copying gives each ResolvedGrouper its own grouper, so a reused grouper instance doesn't carry state from one operation to the next.

A variable can only be rolled along dimensions it actually has. A DataArrayRolling needs at least one of the rolling dims to be in the variable's dims. In `__init__`, each data variable is checked against `self.dim`. The variable gets a DataArrayRolling only if it has some of the rolling dims, and that object is built with just those dims and their window sizes and centers. Variables with none of the rolling dims get no rolling object. Rolling them would fail or be meaningless, because there is no axis to slide a window along. `_dataset_implementation` handles those variables separately. Without explicit labels (UniqueGrouper) or explicit bin edges (BinGrouper with an int), xarray can't know the output groups without reading the chunked data. Finding the unique values or the min/max needed for equal-width bins means computing the array. The check in `ResolvedGrouper.__post_init__` raises a ValueError instead of silently computing it. This keeps the lazy model intact. With explicit labels or bin edges, the group coordinate and the number of groups are known up front. Only the codes are computed lazily, so the graph can be built without loading anything. The old behaviour was to eagerly load the group array. That has been removed, and the error message tells users to call `.compute`/`.load` or pass `labels=` or explicit `bins=`.
